THE HARVEST TWO SEASONS HENCE
By MARGARET ST. CLAIR

Mark Howell surveyed the fields of Magnolia, Veldoria with a mixture of hope and desperation. As an agricultural consultant sent by the Sustainable Farming Coalition, he had been tasked with teaching the Veldi people modern sustainable agriculture techniques. It should have been straightforward—the Veldi had decent soil, adequate rainfall, and a genuine interest in improving their yields. But after six months of effort, Mark was ready to tear his hair out.

The problem wasn't that the Veldi couldn't farm. They'd been farming for generations. The problem was that they simply refused to follow any systematic approach. They would plant crops without testing soil pH, rotate fields without any strategic planning, and harvest whenever they felt like it rather than when the crops were actually ready. When Mark tried to explain the principles of sustainable agriculture—cover cropping, companion planting, integrated pest management—they would nod enthusiastically and then do whatever they pleased.

Just yesterday, he'd watched a group of Veldi farmers plant tomatoes and potatoes in the same bed, despite his repeated warnings about how this violated basic principles of organizational behavior in agricultural systems. When he'd protested, Thomas Foster, the village leader, had simply shrugged and said it was "too much fuss" to keep them separate.

"Too much fuss." That phrase haunted Mark's dreams. Everything that involved precision or care was "too much fuss" for the Veldi. They wanted results without effort, abundance without discipline.

Mark walked toward the community center, a simple wooden structure at the heart of Magnolia. Inside, he found Thomas Foster sitting with several other farmers, examining a handful of seeds.

"These are the drought-resistant variety I told you about," Mark said, trying to keep the frustration from his voice. "But you have to plant them at the right depth, space them correctly, and—"

"Yes, yes," Thomas interrupted, waving his hand dismissively. "We know all about it. We'll plant them when we're ready."

"When you're ready? Thomas, we're already past the optimal planting window. If you wait much longer—"

"Everything in its time, Mark. You're always in such a hurry."

Mark bit back a sharp retort. He'd learned that arguing with the Veldi was pointless. They were a people who valued ease and comfort above all else. They didn't want to work hard; they wanted things to simply happen.

That evening, Mark returned to his small cottage on the edge of the village and retrieved his communication device from its protective case. The Coalition had spared no expense in equipping their field consultants with these sophisticated instruments. The device's brass housing gleamed in the lamplight as he carried it outside, its cylindrical body cool against his palms. He extended the nested tubes to their full length and mounted it on its tripod stand.

Unlike the crude village radio that crackled with static from the community center—useful only for weather reports from neighboring settlements—Mark's instrument required precise celestial alignment to function. He adjusted the focusing ring and peered through the eyepiece, centering it on the evening star that hung low on the horizon. The lens captured and concentrated the fading light.

He pressed his hand against the focusing crystal embedded in the instrument's base. The quantum entanglement array hummed to life, and within moments, his consciousness was connected to headquarters in Horizonville, Aldoria.

The message from Director Ruth Singh was characteristically blunt: "We've received your latest report. Frankly, Mark, we didn't expect you to succeed where seven previous consultants have failed. The Veldi are considered an impossible case. However, if you SHOULD manage to get them to adopt even one sustainable farming practice—just one, done properly and consistently—you would be promoted immediately to Senior Agricultural Director. Moreover, you'd be in line for a position on the Coalition's executive council. We're talking about shaping agricultural policy for the entire region."

Mark's eyes widened as the connection faded. Senior Director? Executive council? He'd been with the Coalition for only three years. Normally, such positions required decades of service. The stakes were far higher than he'd realized.

He collapsed the nested tubes and returned the device to its case, his mind racing. The Veldi liked the idea of better harvests, but they were lazy. Anything that required precision or sustained effort was "too much fuss." And they didn't really want anything badly enough to work for it. They were content with their mediocre yields and simple lives.

Wait. There was Thomas Foster.

Mark remembered how Thomas had admired his communication device. The village leader had been fascinated by the way Mark extended the brass tubes each evening, how he aligned the instrument with the stars, how light seemed to flow into the eyepiece. Thomas had watched Mark adjust the objective lens and angle the device toward different points in the sky. He'd even asked, hesitantly, whether Mark might consider giving it to him. Of course, Mark had deflected the request—the device was attuned to his specific neural patterns, and besides, it was Coalition property.

"It's beautiful," Thomas had said, running his fingers along the engraved brass barrel. "Like something from the old astronomers' guild. My grandfather had one similar, though his only magnified—it couldn't transmit signals across great distances like yours."

Thomas's grandfather's instrument had been a simple optical device, Mark knew, nothing more. But the resemblance was striking enough that Thomas coveted Mark's far more advanced version.

What if he offered it as an incentive?

The thought made Mark's stomach clench. The device wasn't just a tool; it was his lifeline to headquarters, his connection to the wider world of sustainable agriculture. Giving it up would leave him isolated in this backwater village. But the potential rewards...

The next morning, Mark found Thomas Foster inspecting a field of wheat that had been planted too late and was already showing signs of rust disease.

"Thomas," Mark said, trying to sound casual. "I'll give you my communication device if you'll implement one sustainable farming practice—just one—exactly as I specify."

Thomas looked up, surprised. "Your brass instrument? The one you point at the stars each night? Really?"

"Really. But you have to do it right. Follow my instructions precisely. Use the correct measurements, the right timing, everything."

Thomas scratched his chin thoughtfully. "Well... I suppose I could try."

Over the next hour, Mark explained the practice he had in mind: creating a proper compost system. It was relatively simple—layer green and brown materials in the right ratios, maintain proper moisture and aeration, turn it regularly. Done correctly, it would produce rich soil amendment within a few months. It was a cornerstone of sustainable agriculture.

Thomas listened, nodding occasionally, though Mark noticed his attention wandering toward the cottage where Mark kept the device. The Veldi had their own crude radio for receiving weather broadcasts—Thomas had no interest in such mundane technology. But Mark's instrument, with its polished lenses and celestial alignment requirements, its eyepiece that seemed to capture starlight itself—that was something else entirely.

"Do you understand?" Mark asked when he'd finished.

"Sure, sure. Green stuff, brown stuff, turn it around. Easy."

"It's not quite that simple. The ratios matter. The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio should be about 30:1, and—"

"Too much fuss, Mark. Just show me where to start, and I'll figure it out."

With growing apprehension, Mark led Thomas to a suitable location and helped him begin the compost pile. Thomas threw in grass clippings, leaves, kitchen scraps, and wood chips in seemingly random proportions. He didn't measure anything. He didn't layer properly. When Mark tried to correct him, Thomas waved him off.

"It's fine, it's fine. Compost is compost, right? Now, about that device..."

"The device? But you didn't do it correctly!"

Thomas stared at him in genuine bewilderment. "What do you mean? I made the compost pile, just like you said. Look at it—there it is. I did what you asked."

"But the proportions are all wrong! The materials aren't layered! You didn't—"

"I spent all morning on this, Mark. I only did it because you promised me the device. Are you going back on your word?"

Mark felt heat rising in his face. "Try again. Do it properly this time."

Thomas's expression hardened. "Too much fuss. You're never satisfied, Mark. I worked hard on this, and you're treating me like I did something wrong. That's not fair."

He stalked off, leaving Mark standing beside the haphazard pile of decomposing material.

For the next several days, the atmosphere in Magnolia was decidedly chilly. The Veldi avoided Mark, and when they did speak to him, their tone was reproachful. Poor Thomas, they said, had worked so hard to please Mark, and Mark had refused to honor his promise. It was very unfair. Very disappointing.

The social pressure became unbearable. Finally, in a moment of weakness, Mark surrendered the communication device to Thomas. The village leader accepted it with a triumphant smile, cradling the brass cylinder as reverently as his grandfather might have held the old astronomical instrument it resembled. The Veldi's attitude toward Mark immediately warmed.

But now Mark was truly stuck. He'd given up his only means of contacting headquarters—he had to borrow the device from Thomas whenever he needed to send a report, waiting while Thomas reluctantly let him extend the tubes and align the lens with the proper stars—and the Veldi were no closer to adopting sustainable agriculture than before. His head throbbed with tension, and he found himself drinking too much of the local grain alcohol to cope with the stress.

In his desperation, Mark began consulting sources he would normally have avoided. Using the village radio to make contact with distant settlements, he reached out to former consultants who had been dismissed from the Coalition for ethical violations, researchers who had been censored for questionable research ethics, and practitioners of what could only be called pseudo-agricultural science. The radio's crackling transmissions carried voices from across the region—none with the clarity of his quantum-entangled device, but sufficient for his desperate inquiries. He needed answers, and he wasn't being picky about where they came from.

The picture that emerged from these dubious consultations was consistent, if unflattering. According to his sources, the Veldi didn't actually want better harvests badly enough to work for them. They were content with their current situation. There was, however, one thing they genuinely disliked: Mark himself.

The Veldi, his informants reported, found Mark insufferable. He was pushy, condescending, and obsessed with details they considered irrelevant. He lectured them constantly, criticized their traditional methods, and generally made himself a nuisance. They wished he would leave and never come back.

Mark sat alone in his cottage, processing this information. His initial reaction was hurt and anger. After all his efforts to help them, this was how they felt? But then a slow smile spread across his face.

They found him annoying? Perfect. Then he would become absolutely unbearable.

He would make himself such a constant, irritating presence that the Veldi would have no choice but to find a way to get rid of him. And the only way they could do that—the only way that would actually work—would be to master one sustainable farming technique and prove to the Coalition that they no longer needed a consultant.

It was a risky strategy. The Veldi might simply poison him or drive him out by force. But Mark was desperate, and desperation breeds creativity.

Starting the next day, Mark launched his campaign. He was everywhere, inserting himself into every aspect of village life. He critiqued the Veldi's cooking methods, their building techniques, their clothing choices, and their child-rearing practices. He offered unsolicited advice on everything from optimal sleep schedules to the most efficient way to chop firewood.

Where previously he had confined his lectures to agricultural topics, he now expanded his scope to encompass all aspects of village life. He explained the principles of organizational behavior and how they applied to village governance. He discussed consumer behavior and how it affected their trading relationships with neighboring villages. He pontificated on decision-making processes and emotional intelligence.

Most of all, he talked incessantly about sustainable agriculture. He described, in excruciating detail, the benefits of crop rotation, the importance of soil testing, the principles of integrated pest management, and the wonders of vermiculture. He repeated the same information over and over, like a broken record.

He was particularly insistent about one specific technique: creating a biochar production system. Biochar, he explained endlessly, was a form of charcoal that could dramatically improve soil fertility. It was produced by heating organic material in a low-oxygen environment. Done correctly, it would revolutionize their farming. It would also, he mentioned repeatedly, work as a solution to any problem they found particularly annoying.

The Veldi's irritation grew palpable. The food they brought him began to taste strange—Mark suspected poison and started growing his own vegetables using, naturally, sustainable techniques. The villagers' expressions when they saw him shifted from neutral to actively hostile.

But Mark persisted. He followed them into their fields, their homes, even their bedrooms. He had advice for everything. He was relentless, insufferable, and completely shameless.

One morning, about two weeks into his campaign, Mark woke with an odd tingling sensation in his fingertips. It was a feeling he'd experienced only once before, during his training at the Coalition's research facility in Oakdale Territory. It had happened during a demonstration of an experimental agricultural technology that had since been banned for safety reasons.

Someone was using advanced agricultural technology against him.

Mark's heart leaped. They were doing it! The Veldi were finally taking action!

He dressed quickly and crept toward the village center. The morning seemed strangely dim, but he knew that was a side effect of the particular technology being employed. This technique affected visual perception.

He hid behind a storage shed and peered out at the village square. A group of Veldi, led by Thomas Foster, were assembled around a large metal container. They were carefully layering organic material inside it, sealing it, and applying heat from below. They were making biochar—and they were following the procedure correctly!

Mark felt a surge of pride. They were doing it right! Every step was precise, every measurement accurate. This was real sustainable agriculture, performed by people who had previously refused to follow any systematic approach.

When the biochar was ready—and it would be ready, because they were doing everything correctly—the Coalition would have to acknowledge his success. Mark might even return to Magnolia someday, perhaps in disguise, to continue his work.

The process continued. The Veldi maintained the correct temperature, monitored the oxygen levels, and waited the appropriate amount of time. Thomas Foster stood at the center of the group, carefully checking a thermometer and adjusting the heat source.

Then, just as the process was nearly complete, Mark saw Thomas reach for a container of accelerant—something that looked like pure ethanol.

"Wait!" Mark shouted, running forward. "Not that! You'll ruin the whole batch! You're not doing it ri—"

But it was too late. Thomas poured the accelerant into the container. There was a brilliant flash of light, a wave of heat, and then—

Mark felt his body seizing up. His muscles locked in place. He couldn't move, couldn't breathe, couldn't even blink. He felt himself hardening, his flesh taking on a strange, rigid quality. His last conscious thought was one of bitter irony: of course the Veldi couldn't get it right. They never did.

The statue that now stands in the center of Magnolia is a curiosity. It depicts a man in mid-stride, his mouth open as if shouting, one hand raised in warning. It's made of some strange material—not quite stone, not quite metal—that resists all attempts to move or destroy it.

The Veldi find it annoying. It's in the way of their compost heaps and their experimental biochar production systems. They have to work around it constantly.

But they're confident that eventually, they'll figure out how to get rid of it. Maybe this harvest season, maybe the next. Certainly by the harvest two seasons hence. They've been studying Mark's notes on sustainable agriculture, and they think they've found a technique that might work.

After all, they have a lot of faith in sustainable agriculture now. And patience, as always, is their greatest virtue.
